passages.title: Loss and the return to Bethlehem
passages.summary: In the days of the judges a famine strikes Bethlehem. Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and two sons to Moab. He dies, and the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. After about ten years both sons die. Naomi hears there is food in Judah and starts home. She tells her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah leaves, but Ruth promises to share Naomi’s people, God, and grave. They reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Ruth's loyalty and faith during loss. What does Ruth promise in verses 16–17, and what does it cost her?

contextNote.title: A changed name expresses an argument about loss
contextNote.text: Naomi returns to a town that still knows her name (verse 19). She asks to be called Mara, and the verse ties that name to bitterness. She blames the Almighty directly in verses 20–21. She left full, she says, and the LORD brought her back empty. Ruth stands beside her as she says “empty.” The book lets the complaint stand without any rebuke. Verse 22 then quietly adds two things: Ruth and the harvest.

passages.title: Ruth gleans in Boaz’s field
passages.summary: Ruth asks Naomi to let her gather leftover grain behind the harvesters. She happens to come to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. Boaz asks who she is, and the foreman reports her request and steady work. Boaz tells her to stay in his field and drink from his water. He has heard what she did for Naomi. He shares his meal and tells his men to leave extra stalks for her. Ruth carries home a large measure of barley. Naomi blesses Boaz and says he is a close relative.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies kindness and trust. Consider how practical help changes the conditions another person faces. What does Boaz add in verses 15–16 beyond what Ruth asked?

contextNote.title: A harvest rule becomes a means of survival
contextNote.text: The law left the edges of a field for the poor and the foreigner. Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19 state the rule. Ruth is both, and in verse 7 she still asks permission. Verses 9 and 22 show why: a woman alone in a field risked harm. Boaz first gives what the law requires and then more. He orders his men to pull stalks out for her (verse 16). In verse 20 Naomi’s speech changes, and she blesses the LORD’s kindness.

passages.title: The request at the threshing floor
passages.summary: Naomi wants a secure home for Ruth. She sends her to the threshing floor where Boaz winnows barley at night. Ruth washes, dresses, and waits until he has eaten and lies down. She uncovers his feet and lies there. At midnight he wakes and asks who she is. She asks him to spread his garment over her as a near kinsman. Boaz blesses her and promises to act, but a nearer kinsman has first right. He sends her home before dawn with six measures of barley.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: The older Church manual reads Ruth's action as a request for marriage. How do Ruth’s words in verse 9 differ from Naomi’s plan in verse 4?

contextNote.title: Ruth gives the plan her own words
contextNote.text: Naomi’s plan ends with Boaz telling Ruth what to do (verse 4). In verse 9 Ruth tells Boaz what to do. She asks for his covering and gives the reason: he is a near kinsman. That ties her marriage to his family duty toward Naomi’s house. In 2:12 Boaz prayed that the LORD would shelter her. Now she asks him to be that shelter. Boaz calls her request a kindness and names her a worthy woman (verses 10–11).

passages.title: The gate agreement and Obed’s birth
passages.summary: Boaz sits at the town gate and stops the nearer kinsman. He gathers ten elders as witnesses. He says Naomi is selling Elimelech’s field, and the man agrees to buy it. Boaz adds that the buyer must marry Ruth and raise an heir for the dead. The man withdraws and hands over his sandal to confirm it. Boaz declares that he has bought the land and taken Ruth as his wife. Ruth bears Obed, and the women tell Naomi her life is restored. Obed becomes the grandfather of David.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares Boaz’s care with Jesus Christ’s power to redeem, or save. How does Boaz help Ruth and Naomi?

contextNote.title: Care requires a public commitment
contextNote.text: The gate is the town’s court, and ten elders make the act public. The nearer kinsman accepts the field (verse 4) and refuses Ruth (verse 6). A son by Ruth would carry Mahlon’s name and inherit the land. Boaz accepts that cost in verses 9–10 before witnesses. The man who guarded his own estate is never named in the book. A cuneiform tablet shows how another people recorded a field sale. The women tell Naomi that Ruth is better than seven sons (verse 15).

words.label: Redeem
words.meaning: To buy back a person or property. The word is also used for God’s rescue of people.

words.label: Kinsman
words.meaning: A near relative. In Ruth, a near kinsman may buy back a relative’s land.

words.label: Anoint
words.meaning: To pour oil on a person or thing to set it apart. Kings and priests were anointed.

words.label: Ephah
words.meaning: A dry measure of about 22 liters.
